{
"Object-Oriented Design": "A software design paradigm that models systems as collections of interacting objects, each encapsulating state and behavior, organized through principles such as inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation.",
"Inheritance": "A mechanism by which one class derives attributes and behaviors from another, enabling the modeling of hierarchical relationships and reuse of existing code.",
"Composition": "A design technique in which complex objects are constructed by combining simpler component objects, favoring flexible assembly of behavior over rigid inheritance hierarchies.",
"Encapsulation": "The principle of bundling data and the methods that operate on it within a single unit while restricting external access to internal implementation details.",
"Polymorphism": "The ability for objects of different types to be treated through a common interface, allowing a single operation to behave differently based on the underlying object's type.",
"Interface": "A formal specification of methods and behaviors that a class must provide, defining a contract without prescribing how it is implemented.",
"Contract": "An agreement specifying the expected inputs, outputs, and behaviors of a software component, which implementations must honor to ensure correct interaction.",
"Implementation": "The concrete realization of an interface or abstract specification, providing the actual code and logic that fulfills defined behaviors.",
"Class Hierarchy": "A tree-like structure of classes connected by inheritance relationships, representing generalization and specialization among types.",
"Derived Class": "A class that inherits attributes and behaviors from a base class, potentially extending or overriding them to specialize its functionality.",
"Base Class": "A class from which other classes inherit, providing common attributes and behaviors that derived classes can reuse or refine.",
"Liskov Substitution Principle": "A SOLID principle stating that objects of a derived class must be substitutable for objects of its base class without altering the correctness of the program.",
"Type": "A classification that defines the structure, behavior, and permissible operations of a set of values or objects in a program.",
"Object": "An instance of a class that encapsulates state through its attributes and exhibits behavior through its methods.",
"SOLID Principle": "A set of five object-oriented design principles—Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion—that promote maintainable and extensible software.",
"Abstraction": "The process of exposing only essential characteristics of an entity while hiding irrelevant details, enabling simplified modeling and interaction with complex systems."
}
